title: Cases of suspected spiking at the emergency department - toxicology, phenomenology and psychological sequalae
summary:
This study examines people who present to an emergency department with suspected 'spiking'. They have been unintentionally administered psychoactive substances, often with the aim of incapacitating them. The frequency of spiking in Germany is currently unknown, and the psychological consequences and necessary aftercare are still unclear.

People who think they have been spiked or for whom there is clinical suspicion can take part. After the suspected incident, they should contact an emergency department within 12 hours to have blood and urine samples analyzed. An interview will be conducted about the incident, both 4 weeks and 6 months afterwards. Information on substance use, psychological stress (depression, anxiety, trauma-related symptoms) and the need for follow-up care is recorded.

The overall aim is to gain insights into the frequency of spiking, the substances involved and their effects on mental health. It is assumed that spiking is only confirmed in a small percentage of suspected cases. In addition, it is assumed that many subjects have a detectable alcohol intoxication and that their blood alcohol level is above the calculated amount in many cases. It is assumed that many people have intentionally consumed at least two psychoactive substances.

interventions.name: Adults of all genders who present to a Berlin emergency department with suspected spiking receive  toxicological testing (T0) and are interviewed and questioned 3-7 days after the event (T1), as well as after 4 weeks (T2) and 6 months (T3).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Presumed spiking occurred ≤ 12 hours before presentation at emergency department
Exclusion criteria:
none
